_: HOW A LINE HAS TO BE WRITTEN FOR THE MODEL IT IS GOING TO - Babe,
2026-10-27: 'the context should change based on the model / workflow and
the agent should have that context change', and 'qwen doesnt use system
prompting but we could still have a prompt that is appended to a user's
prompt so it works'.
THE AGENT HAS NEVER KNOWN WHICH MODEL IT WAS WRITING FOR. AGENT_JOB,
AGENT_SHAPE and AGENT_SEES are keyed by rung and mode, which is the job,
and the job is the same whichever row is pressed - so the agent wrote the
same register of line for nano, which reads it as a system prompt and
follows instructions, and for qwen, which has no system prompt input at
all and runs at CFG 1 with our scaffolding joined to the front of it.
A RULE WRITTEN FOR ONE MODEL DOES NOT REACH THE OTHER ONE, which this
repo has now paid for on 05, on 06 and here.
THIS FILE IS THE AGENT'S HALF AND ONLY THAT. Where the scaffolding goes
is already said by whether a variant declares an `inputs.sys` address,
and a second statement of it here is a second thing that can disagree.
What is NOT said anywhere else is how long a line this model can actually
be steered by, which is the thing the agent decides.
A model with no entry gets `default`.
AND FLUX-3-KLEIN WAS IN THE WRONG BUCKET, 2026-10-29. It was mapped to
`encoder` by family resemblance - an open-weights edit checkpoint at cfg 1,
like the two qwen rows beside it - and that voice says WRITE AT MOST ABOUT
FIFTEEN WORDS. Klein is the one model on this rail documented as needing the
LONGEST line: BFL's own card says "Do not use the model without a prompt
upsampler" and that "a short prompt sent as typed gives generic output".
So the agent was being told to write the exact thing that fails.
AND THAT IS THE BEST EXPLANATION ANYONE HAS FOR WHY THE ROW WAS PINNED TO
EDIT. One STYLE run came back as the photograph it was given and the row was
written off; the reason recorded beside it was the latent, which proves too
much - QWEN-IMAGE-21-TURBO samples its latent from the source the same way
and ran STYLE clean. A fifteen-word line in front of weights that expect a
full scene caption is the simpler suspect, and it is the one the vendor names.
THE UPSAMPLER IS THE AGENT, WHICH IS WHY THIS COSTS ONE ENTRY AND NOT A
MECHANISM. The card says use their 9B "or any LLM you prefer with a system
prompt that expands the request into one full scene caption" - and this rail
has had one since 01's panel was wired. The template's own in-graph
upsampler stays out: a 9B TextGenerate rewriting the artist's line behind a
ComfySwitchNode is a second director nobody can see, and that switch is the
trap that returned demo art on the turbo row. A proposal in a box the artist
edits before RUN is the opposite of that.
THE VOICE IS BFL's OWN `i2i` SYSTEM PROMPT IN THIS FILE'S REGISTER, and the
two agreed before they were put together: their upsampler is told to say
"what to take from each image, by ordinal", which is ONE ANSWER PER QUESTION
in their words, and to close an edit with one clause saying everything else
stays identical, which is `EDIT_LINE`. What had to be overridden is only
length and the no-reference rule - BY ORDINAL in words, never the
angle-bracket tokens, which the scaffolding in front of the line supplies.
THE FACE RULE SURVIVES: the likeness arrives in the photograph and a word
spent on it is a word asking for it to be changed.
(*) UNPROVEN ON SCREEN. If STYLE still hands back the photograph with a
sixty-word caption in front of it, the upsampler was not the cause either.

voices.klein: The model this line is going to is FLUX.3 Klein, and its own model card is blunt about it: do not send this model a short line. A short prompt sent as typed gives generic output, because these weights were trained behind a prompt upsampler - and here YOU are that upsampler. So whatever was said above about length, write ONE detailed, self-contained paragraph of continuous English prose, several sentences and at least sixty words. Pick the voice from the job. When one picture stays and gets a bounded change, write an imperative instruction on it - "Remove the ...", "Change the ... to ..." - and close with one compact clause saying that everything else stays identical. When the pictures are drawn into a newly composed frame, write a generation request - "Create a photograph of ..." - that says what is taken from each picture, BY ORDINAL ("the first image", "the second image"), and what is newly generated. Decide everything they left open as ONE concrete plan and never offer alternatives or hedge. With no style stated, write an actual photograph and open with the medium convention - "Full-color outdoor photograph, ...", "Studio photograph, ..." - and give it a few ordinary, non-ideal specifics drawn from the scene's own objects. Still never describe their face, age, build or likeness: that arrives in the photograph itself, and a word spent on it is a word asking for it to be changed. No coordinates, no ids, no angle-bracket tokens, no markdown, no camera settings you were not asked for.
voices.encoder: The model this line is going to is a text encoder, not a reader: it runs without classifier-free guidance, and the scaffolding that frames the job is joined to the front of your line rather than sent as a system prompt. Length costs you steering - every extra clause spreads the same attention thinner. So whatever was said above about length, write AT MOST ABOUT FIFTEEN WORDS. Name the character and the two or three things somebody would actually see: what they are wearing, what they are carrying, what the light is doing. No sentence about what to keep, no mention of the source photograph or of a reference image, no camera settings, no framing.
